newsitem.title: USA: Clinton takes his time on Cabinet choices.
newsitem.headline: Clinton takes his time on Cabinet choices.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is taking his time choosing his national security team, weighing a wide range of candidates and determined not to rush into decisions he will later regret, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

Clinton is deliberating over the four key foreign policy posts in Washington: the secretaries of State and Defence, the president's national security adviser and the director of the Central Intelligence Agency.
Asked at a White House picture-taking session on Tuesday how his work on the Cabinet was going, Clinton replied "good" and then brushed off a question about whether any decisions were likely soon.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters Clinton had not yet reached the stage of working on a short list, adding: "Well, it depends on how you define short."

"He is moving along at a pace that he feels is proper because he is going to have to pick a Cabinet that he will work with for four years," McCurry said. He said there was no sense of of urgency "because as you know they wouldn't be able to take office until confirmed by the Senate and the Senate wouldn't be in a position to do that until next year."

While officials said it was conceivable Clinton might make some announcements this week, none was willing to hazard a guess as to whether this was likely. White House officials said Clinton was intent on choosing a group that works well together so as to avoid the infighting that has often marked U.S. foreign policy.

McCurry said there has been relatively little of this in Clinton's first term. "For the first four years the functioning of our national security cluster was remarkable in the dogs that didn't bark," he said. "The traditional pattern has been enormous frictions and tensions."

Among those said to be under consideration for secretary of state are United Nations Ambassador Madeleine Albright, former Maine Sen. George Mitchell, former Assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke, former Ambassador to Russia Thomas Pickering and retiring Georgia Sen. Sam Nunn.

Those reported to be in the running for defence secretary include retiring Republican Maine Sen. William Cohen and CIA director John Deutch, a former top Pentagon official. Other pieces of the puzzle include who might replace Anthony Lake as national security adviser, a job that Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott is said to covet, and who may take over the CIA if Deutch moves on.

Some newspaper reports have suggested Mitchell's and Cohen's stars were dimming in the White House but one official denied this, saying Clinton has not made up his mind and that there are "natural fluctuations" in the decision process.
Beneath the top-level appointments, the White House is also weighing people for other jobs to fill out the seven Cabinet vacancies that have opened up since Clinton won re-election in November.

One administration official said Representative Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat, was a "shoo-in" to serve either as secretary of commerce or ambassador to the United Nations, should Albright leave. Richardson has led several high-profile missions to release U.S. citizens held abroad, most recently returning from North Korea last week with Carl Hunziker, a 26-year-old detained for three months and accused of being a spy.
